title: Read-write lock
points: A read-write lock allows many readers at the same time but only one writer, and a writer excludes all readers.
It only helps when reads are heavy and writes are rare.
If writes are frequent, writers keep waiting for readers and the extra bookkeeping makes it slower than a plain lock.
trade: Use for read-mostly data such as config or a cache. Versus a plain lock: more concurrency for reads, more overhead per acquire. Versus an atomic variable: handles multi-variable state but is heavier.
test: A product catalog is read thousands of times per second and updated a few times a day. Which lock fits, and what would make it a bad choice?
answer: A read-write lock: readers run in parallel. It becomes a bad choice if writes become frequent, since writers wait on readers and the overhead outweighs the gain.

questions.question: A cache is updated on almost every request. Is a read-write lock a good fit?
options: Yes, readers always run in parallel
No, with frequent writes the writers wait for readers and a plain lock is just as good or better
Yes, it removes the need for any other lock
questions.explanation: The benefit comes from many concurrent readers. With many writes the benefit disappears and overhead remains.

questions.question: What does a read-write lock allow?
options: Many readers at once, or one exclusive writer
Only one thread at a time
Readers and a writer at the same time
questions.explanation: Readers share the lock; a writer needs exclusive access.
